extracted.intended_audience: Congress, USPTO stakeholders, patent policy makers, patent practitioners, industry commenters (life sciences and computer/AI sectors)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary and evaluation of public views on U.S. patent-eligibility jurisprudence (Mayo/Alice) and its impacts across sectors, with emphasis on computer-related inventions/AI and life sciences. Covers empirical metrics, stakeholder concerns, and suggested desiderata for an eligibility standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, predictability, and consistent application of eligibility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "The standard for determining whether an invention is eligible for patenting should be clear, predictable, and consistently applied."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders broadly agreed on this desideratum. Slides note calls for legal clarity and certainty; criticisms of current jurisprudence emphasize inconsistencies, unpredictability, and uncertainty in issuance and enforcement of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo–Alice two-step test and 'significantly more' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the Mayo and Alice framework, including the second element inquiry of whether the claimed invention is 'significantly more' than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters identified difficulties with applying the second element; several noted challenges determining whether a claim supplies 'significantly more' and how that should be evaluated in different technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a uniform definition of 'abstract idea'
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no uniform definition of an abstract idea, which complicates application of the Mayo/Alice framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters highlighted that lack of a consistent definition undermines predictable outcomes; this is a focal point for disputes in computer-implemented inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim provides a technical solution to a technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether a claimed invention provides a technical solution to a technical problem can support a finding of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters provided examples where the eligibility test showed a claimed invention provides a technical solution; this is cited as a way to distinguish patentable computer-implemented inventions from abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether computer-implemented elements (calculations, simulations, models, instruction sets) are patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that computer-implemented inventions often comprise calculations, simulations, models, instruction sets, etc., which commenters noted are not patentable by themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders debated how to treat such elements in claims and whether their inclusion can render a claim patent-eligible; impacts heavily discussed for AI and software-related patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on investment and innovation (including sector-specific investment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether subject-matter jurisprudence negatively impacts investment in innovation and continued investment in fields like AI and genomics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some stakeholders argued data do not support a negative impact on investment; slides cite investment numbers (e.g., US AI investment $23.6B Q2 2021; genomics investment growth) to argue continued strong investment despite jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO allowance rates as an empirical metric (AI vs non-AI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance rate for patent applications, particularly observed decreases for applications containing AI following Alice relative to non-AI applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slides present observed data: AI-containing application allowance rates stayed below non-AI rates until 2019, then increased ~8% consistent with 2019 USPTO examiner guidance reducing eligibility rejections in Alice-affected technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impacts on particular innovation sectors (life sciences and computer-related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how eligibility jurisprudence alters the landscape differently across sectors, with particular impacts on life sciences and computer-related industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation emphasizes distinct sectoral impacts: life sciences claim heavy reliance on patents to recoup R&D costs; computer-related industries emphasize tools to curb overly broad patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of patent protection to recoup life sciences R&D investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether patent protection is sufficient to allow life sciences companies to recoup substantial R&D investments (e.g., ~$2.6 billion and ~12 years to bring a medicine to market).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life sciences commenters stressed reliance on patents; examples given of diagnostic claims granted abroad but rejected in the U.S. on eligibility grounds, arguing this divergence harms companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative divergence with other jurisdictions (diagnostics protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether U.S. patent-eligibility standards diverge from other countries, particularly affecting protection for medical diagnostics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters presented examples of diagnostic claims allowed outside the U.S. but rejected domestically; this cross-jurisdictional comparison used as a criterion for evaluating adequacy of U.S. policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on access to testing, medicine, and downstream public-health outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether current jurisprudence facilitates better access to testing and medicines or, conversely, restricts access and impairs research and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters applauded jurisprudence for improving access; others warned restricting access to gene sequences impairs R&D. Data cited (e.g., genomics investment growth post-Myriad) used to contest economic-harm claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on small and medium enterprises (SMEs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of how eligibility jurisprudence impacts SMEs' ability to innovate, compete, and rely on patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slides list impacts on SMEs as a recurring topic in comments; specific harms or benefits were raised but not uniformly resolved in the summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal costs and predictability of enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of legal costs associated with patent prosecution and litigation under current eligibility rules and resulting unpredictability in enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders listed legal costs among key concerns; unpredictable eligibility outcomes can increase litigation and prosecution costs and affect market behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to technical information (disclosure vs exclusivity balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether jurisprudence affects the public's access to technical information (e.g., via patents' disclosure function) and the balance between exclusivity and dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders raised access to technical information as a dimension of impact; some argued narrower eligibility increases public access, while others pointed to harms from reduced protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the eligibility standard to address overly broad patents and PAEs (patent assertion entities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the current eligibility framework serves as a useful tool to address overly broad patents and defend against abusive lawsuits by patent assertion entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters (primarily from computer-related industries) asserted that the new eligibility standard helps curb overly broad claims and abusive enforcement; this is cited as a pro-eligibility-restriction rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: National security and U.S. competitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate impacts of eligibility jurisprudence on national security interests and the international competitiveness of U.S. innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slides list national security and U.S. competitiveness among stakeholder concerns; commenters argued the U.S. remains preferred for AI investment despite eligibility debate, but competitiveness remains a policy consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of USPTO guidance (e.g., 2019 examiner guidance) in shaping outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether USPTO examiner guidance can reduce subject-matter-eligibility rejections and increase allowance rates in affected technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation links the 2019 USPTO examiner guidance to a substantial reduction in rejections in Alice-affected technologies and to later increases in allowance rates for AI applications.
